title: Git: Commands and Concepts

sources.name: Original educational writing from general knowledge
Official Git reference manuals: command reference and switch/restore behavior (factual checks; no copied prose)

description: For Git beginners learning snapshots, staging, branches, collaboration, and recovery. Commands use uppercase placeholders such as PATH; cards explain when an operation discards changes or rewrites history.

cards.front: What is Git?
cards.back: A distributed version-control system that records project history as commits and supports parallel development.

cards.front: What is a Git repository?
cards.back: The object database and references that store a project's version history and related metadata.

cards.front: What is the working tree?
cards.back: The checked-out files and directories you edit.

cards.front: What is the staging area, also called the index?
cards.back: The proposed snapshot that will normally become the next commit.

cards.front: What is a commit?
cards.back: A recorded snapshot with metadata and parent references, identified by an object ID.

cards.front: What is a branch in Git?
cards.back: A movable reference to a commit, normally advanced by new commits on that branch.

cards.front: What does HEAD usually refer to?
cards.back: The currently checked-out branch, or directly to a commit in detached-HEAD state.

cards.front: What is a remote?
cards.back: A named configuration for another repository's location and associated fetch or push settings.

cards.front: What is the conventional meaning of the remote name origin?
cards.back: It is the default remote name commonly created by clone; it has no special built-in ownership meaning.

cards.front: Which command initializes a repository in the current directory?
Which command creates a local copy of a repository at a URL?
Which command shows the working-tree and staging-area status?
Which command gives a compact status display?
Which command stages a specific file's current contents?
Does git add permanently track future edits to a file in the next commit?
cards.back: No. It stages the file's contents at that moment; later edits must be staged again to enter that commit.

cards.front: Which command stages additions, modifications, and deletions throughout the working tree?
Which command interactively stages selected changes as hunks?
Which command creates a commit from the staged snapshot with a message?
What does git commit -a include automatically?
cards.back: Modifications and deletions of already tracked files; it does not automatically include new untracked files.

cards.front: Which command displays unstaged changes to tracked files?
Which command displays staged changes relative to HEAD?
Which command displays tracked-file changes in the working tree relative to HEAD, combining staged and unstaged effects?
Which command shows commit history reachable from the current commit?
Which command shows one compact line per commit?
Which command displays an ASCII graph with compact commit history and references across branches?
Which command shows a commit's details and patch?
Which command shows the most recent commit's details?
What does HEAD~1 denote?
cards.back: The first parent of HEAD, one generation back along the first-parent chain.

cards.front: What does HEAD~2 denote?
cards.back: The first parent's first parent of HEAD, two generations back along the first-parent chain.

cards.front: What does HEAD^2 denote for a merge commit?
cards.back: Its second parent, if it has one.

cards.front: Which command lists local branches?
Which command lists local and remote-tracking branches?
Which command creates a branch without switching to it?
Which command switches to an existing branch?
Which command creates a new branch and switches to it?
Which command switches back to the previously checked-out branch or location?
Which command renames the current branch?
Which command deletes a local branch with the usual merged-history safety check?
How does git branch -D differ from git branch -d?
cards.back: It forces local branch deletion without requiring the merged-history check to pass.

cards.front: Which command merges another branch into the current branch?
What is a fast-forward merge?
cards.back: A merge that advances the current branch reference to a descendant commit without creating a merge commit.

cards.front: What is a merge commit?
cards.back: A commit with multiple parents that records the joining of histories.

cards.front: Which option requests a merge commit even when a fast-forward would be possible?
Which command allows a merge only if it can fast-forward?
What is a merge conflict?
cards.back: A situation in which Git cannot automatically reconcile competing changes and needs a resolution.

cards.front: What do conflict markers such as <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> indicate?
cards.back: Alternative conflicting file sections that must be edited into the intended final content, with the markers removed.

cards.front: After resolving conflicted files in a normal merge, how do you complete it?
cards.back: Stage the resolved files with git add, then run git commit or git merge --continue.

cards.front: Which command attempts to abandon an in-progress merge?
cards.back: git merge --abort; restoring the exact prior state can be difficult if pre-existing uncommitted changes were mixed into the merge.

cards.front: Which command downloads remote objects and updates remote-tracking references without integrating them into the current branch?
What does git pull do conceptually?
cards.back: Fetches and then integrates the selected upstream history, using merge or rebase according to options and configuration.

cards.front: Which command requests a fetch followed by rebasing the current branch onto its upstream?
Which command pushes a local branch and sets its upstream relationship?
Which command lists configured remotes and their fetch/push URLs?
Which command adds a remote named upstream?
Which command changes the URL of origin?
What is a remote-tracking branch such as origin/main?
cards.back: A local reference recording the last fetched state of a branch at that remote; it is not a live connection.

cards.front: What is an upstream branch?
cards.back: The branch configured as the current branch's default comparison and integration target for commands such as pull and status.

cards.front: Which command sets an existing local branch to track origin/main?
Which command deletes a branch from a remote?
cards.back: git push origin --delete BRANCH; this changes the remote repository and should be coordinated with collaborators.

cards.front: Which command prunes stale remote-tracking references during a fetch?
What is rebasing?
cards.back: Replaying commits onto a new base, usually creating new commit objects with different IDs.

cards.front: Which command rebases the current branch onto main?
Why should rebasing already shared commits be coordinated?
cards.back: It rewrites commit identities, so collaborators may need to reconcile their histories.

cards.front: Which command continues a paused rebase after conflicts are resolved and staged?
Which command abandons an in-progress rebase?
Which command opens an interactive rebase for the last three first-parent commits in a simple linear history?
What does squash do in an interactive rebase?
cards.back: Combines a commit with the preceding retained commit and allows their messages to be combined or edited.

cards.front: What does fixup normally do in an interactive rebase?
cards.back: Combines a commit with the preceding retained commit while discarding the fixup commit's message.

cards.front: Which command applies the change introduced by a selected commit onto the current branch?
Which command creates a new commit that reverses the changes of an earlier ordinary commit?
How does revert differ from reset when undoing a shared change?
cards.back: Revert adds a compensating commit; reset moves a reference and can remove commits from the branch's visible history.

cards.front: What does git reset --soft COMMIT change?
cards.back: It moves the current branch or HEAD to the target while leaving the index and working tree unchanged.

cards.front: What does git reset --mixed COMMIT change?
cards.back: It moves the current branch or HEAD and resets the index to the target, leaving working-tree files unchanged.

cards.front: What does git reset --hard COMMIT change?
cards.back: It resets the current branch or HEAD, index, and tracked working-tree state to the target; uncommitted changes can be lost and obstructing untracked paths can be removed.

cards.front: Which command unstages a file while keeping its working-tree edits in a repository with a HEAD commit?
What does git restore PATH normally do without --staged or --source?
cards.back: It replaces the working-tree version with the index version, discarding unstaged changes to that path.

cards.front: Which command restores a working-tree file from a specified commit without staging it by default?
Which command removes a tracked file and stages its deletion?
Which command stops tracking a file while leaving its working-tree copy?
Which command moves a tracked file and stages the corresponding path changes?
What does a .gitignore file specify?
cards.back: Patterns for intentionally untracked files that Git should generally omit from untracked-file reporting and ordinary add operations.

cards.front: Does adding a tracked file to .gitignore stop tracking it?
cards.back: No. It must be removed from the index separately if tracking should stop.

cards.front: Where can you put repository-local ignore patterns without committing them?
cards.back: In .git/info/exclude, or its corresponding Git-directory location.

cards.front: Which command reports the ignore rule affecting an untracked path?
Which command saves tracked working-tree and index changes in a stash?
Which stash option also includes untracked files?
cards.back: git stash push -u; ignored files are not included by this option.

cards.front: Which command lists stash entries?
How do git stash apply and git stash pop differ?
cards.back: Apply restores a stash while retaining the entry; pop restores it and removes the entry if application succeeds.

cards.front: Which command deletes a selected stash entry without applying it?
Which command lists local tags?
Which command creates an annotated tag with a message?
How does an annotated tag differ from a lightweight tag?
cards.back: An annotated tag has its own object with metadata and a message; a lightweight tag is a direct reference to an object.

cards.front: Which command explicitly pushes one tag to origin?
What is detached HEAD state?
cards.back: HEAD points directly to a commit rather than to a local branch reference.

cards.front: How can you retain new detached-HEAD commits on a named branch?
cards.back: Create a branch at the current commit, for example with git switch -c NAME.

cards.front: Which command shows local reference movement history useful for finding a recent lost commit?
Why is reflog not a permanent backup?
cards.back: Reflog entries expire, unreachable objects can be pruned, and reflogs are normally local rather than shared by push.

cards.front: Which command searches tracked file contents for a pattern?
Which command shows the commit and author most recently responsible for each line of a file?
cards.back: git blame PATH; it describes line attribution in history, not personal fault.

cards.front: What does git bisect help locate?
cards.back: The commit that introduced a behavior by repeatedly testing commits between known good and bad endpoints.

cards.front: Which commands start a basic bisect session and mark known endpoints?
cards.back: git bisect start, git bisect bad BAD_COMMIT, and git bisect good GOOD_COMMIT.

cards.front: Which command ends a bisect session and restores the original checkout position?
Which command previews untracked files and directories that a clean would remove?
cards.back: git clean -nd; inspect the preview carefully before considering a destructive clean.

cards.front: Why is git push --force-with-lease generally safer than unconditional --force?
cards.back: It checks an expected remote reference value before rewriting it, but still rewrites shared history and requires coordination.

cards.front: Which command sets a repository-local author name for future commits?
Which command sets a repository-local author email for future commits?
What does the --global option do in git config?
cards.back: It writes to the user's global Git configuration rather than only the current repository's configuration.

cards.front: Which command shows where configuration values came from?
What does git commit --amend do?
cards.back: Creates a replacement for the latest commit using the staged snapshot and selected message; its commit ID changes.

cards.front: Does committing automatically send changes to a remote repository?
cards.back: No. A commit is local; pushing is a separate operation.
